common_name: Viola Klose Salvia (Exceptionally Dark Violet-Blue Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Viola Klose is prized among meadow sage cultivars for flowers in an especially deep, saturated violet-blue that reads almost black-purple in low light.

directions: This German-raised meadow sage selection is grown for flower spikes in an unusually deep violet-blue, noticeably darker and more saturated than Caradonna or May Night, packed densely along upright stems above aromatic, wrinkled gray-green foliage. Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; like other nemorosa cultivars it resents heavy, wet winter soil and performs best where drainage is reliable. Shear the spent flower spikes back by about half once the first flush fades to tidy the clump and encourage a second, lighter round of bloom later in the season. Its dark coloring makes it a strong anchor for pairing with silver foliage, pale yellow, or white-flowered companions at the front or middle of a sunny perennial border.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Lubecca Salvia (Compact Uniform Violet-Blue Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Lubecca forms an exceptionally uniform, dwarf, well-branched mound that holds its shape without flopping, making it a popular choice for mass plantings and pots as well as borders.

directions: Lubecca is a German-bred dwarf meadow sage selected for a tight, even mound habit and heavy flowering, sending up short violet-blue spikes densely over the compact, wrinkled gray-green foliage from late spring into summer. Grow it in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, where its naturally uniform size keeps plantings neat without staking or frequent division. Cutting the first flush of spent spikes back encourages a reliable second round of bloom and keeps the mound from looking tired by midsummer. Its small, predictable footprint makes it a dependable choice for edging sunny beds, mass landscape plantings, and large containers where taller nemorosa cultivars would be out of scale.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after frost danger passes into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Strata is an All-America Selections winner noted for a distinctive two-tone spike where silvery-white calyxes contrast with true-blue florets.

directions: Strata earned All-America Selections honors for its striking bicolor flower spikes, where the silvery-white calyxes stay showy even as the true-blue corollas drop, giving each spike a frosted, two-toned look unlike most other mealycup sage selections. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained, average soil in full sun once danger of frost has passed. It blooms heavily from early summer through fall with excellent heat and drought tolerance once established, and its narrow, upright habit holds up well without staking in beds, borders, or containers. Deadhead spent spikes to keep plants tidy and encourage continued flowering through the season.

common_name: Vista Purple Salvia (Early-Flowering Compact Bedding Salvia)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after all danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Vista Purple shares the branching, well-filled habit of the Vista series, flowering earlier and more densely than older tall splendens strains.

directions: Vista Purple is a compact, heavily branching member of the Vista bedding salvia series, bearing dense spikes of rich violet-purple flowers from early summer through frost on plants well-filled from the base. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since it needs a long season to size up, and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade after frost danger has passed. It tolerates summer heat better than older tall Salvia splendens strains and keeps flowering steadily with regular watering and occasional deadheading of spent spikes. In zone 9 it can persist as a short-lived perennial in sheltered, frost-free microclimates, but it is most reliably grown as a warm-season annual.
sources: Pennsylvania State University Extension — Annual Trial Gardens

common_name: Vista Salmon Salvia (Early-Flowering Compact Bedding Salvia)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after all danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Vista Salmon offers a softer salmon-pink flower color within the same early-flowering, well-branched Vista series.

directions: Vista Salmon brings a softer salmon-pink flower color to the compact, well-branched Vista bedding salvia series, filling out densely from the base and covering itself in flower spikes from early summer through frost. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost to give it time to reach flowering size, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade once frost danger has passed. Its muted, warm-toned flowers pair more easily with pastel companions than the more common scarlet-red bedding salvias, and the compact habit needs no staking. Water regularly through summer heat and deadhead spent spikes occasionally to keep the planting flowering steadily until frost.
sources: Pennsylvania State University Extension — Annual Trial Gardens

common_name: Dear Anja Salvia (Compact Deep Violet-Blue Hybrid Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Dear Anja is a compact hybrid meadow sage raised in Europe, similar in character to Blue Hill and May Night but kept noticeably shorter and tidier.

directions: Dear Anja is a compact European hybrid meadow sage carrying dense, upright spikes of deep violet-blue flowers over aromatic, wrinkled gray-green foliage from late spring into summer. Grow it in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun, where its tidy, self-supporting habit stays neat without staking even after heavy rain. Shearing back the spent flower spikes once the first flush fades typically prompts a second, lighter round of bloom later in the season. Its naturally compact size suits the front of a sunny perennial border, edging, or containers, and the long bloom period draws bees steadily through the growing season.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
